extracted.intended_audience: students and early-career mathematicians (undergraduates, graduate students, postdocs) and those seeking academic career advice in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: General-purpose career advice and practical guidelines for training, research, presentation, and time-management aimed at students and early-career researchers in mathematics. Covers stage-by-stage recommendations (undergraduate, graduate, postdoc) plus related study and productivity tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss major career decisions with your advisor
rubrics_metrics.description: The advice here is very generic in nature; I don’t pretend to have any sort of “silver bullet” ... You will of course need to evaluate many factors, contexts, and needs specific to your own situation, ... I would in particular recommend discussing such decisions with your advisor if you have one, as he or she will be familiar with your situation and will likely be able to provide pertinent advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the page as general guidance only; for important career choices solicit personalized advice from your advisor who knows your circumstances. Evaluate contextual factors and apply common sense before making major decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard, work professionally, and enjoy your work
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to work hard, and work professionally. But it is also important to enjoy your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance sustained, disciplined effort and professional behaviour with finding aspects of research you enjoy; productivity and professionalism matter, but so does long-term enjoyment to sustain a career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think ahead; ask dumb questions to learn the road forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Think ahead to understand the way forward; ask yourself dumb questions to understand the way before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan research trajectories by anticipating future steps; deliberately ask simple/basic questions about the direction you plan to take to reveal hidden difficulties and to clarify the path forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related to your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conferences and seminars to broaden perspective, find collaborators, and get exposure to techniques and problems beyond your immediate area; don't restrict attendance only to perfectly aligned topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your advisor but take the initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to your advisor, but also take the initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regular communication with your supervisor while proactively seeking problems, resources, and collaborators; avoid passivity—combine guidance from advisor with independent initiative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prematurely obsessing on a single "big problem" or big theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t prematurely obsess on a single “big problem” or “big theory”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In early stages avoid locking into one grand problem that may be unrealistic; develop breadth, try multiple directions, and let strong projects emerge organically rather than committing too early to one risky pursuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down what you've done and make your work available
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down what you’ve done, and make your work available. In this regard, I have some advice on how to write and submit papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record progress, prepare written notes and papers, and disseminate results (preprints, arXiv, journals). Making work available raises visibility, helps get feedback, and is essential to an academic career; follow best practices for writing and submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and relearn your field; be willing to learn outside your field
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and relearn your field, but don’t be afraid to learn things outside your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuously refresh core knowledge while staying open to new areas and techniques that may benefit your research; cross-disciplinary learning can provide powerful tools and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the limitations of your tools and the power of others' tools; aim just beyond your range
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the limitations of your tools, but also learn the power of other mathematician’s tools. In particular, you should continually aim just beyond your current range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be self-aware about what techniques you can and cannot use; study complementary methods used by others and stretch yourself by tackling problems slightly beyond current abilities to foster growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and patient in research
rubrics_metrics.description: In your research, be both flexible and patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect setbacks, change directions when warranted, and allow time for ideas to mature; flexibility and patience help you adapt to the long-term nature of mathematical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and present research when possible; tailor talks to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You should definitely travel and present your research if given the opportunity. But be considerate of your audience; talks are not the same as papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take opportunities to present work (conferences, seminars) to increase visibility and get feedback. Prepare talks specifically for the audience (different goals and levels than written papers); adapt content, give exposition, and emphasize intuition where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work; don't be afraid to discard ideas (use the wastebasket)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of your own work, and don’t be afraid to use the wastebasket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate your arguments and results; cut or shelve unpromising lines of inquiry to avoid wasting time and to keep the research program focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch low-intensity tasks together to reduce distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Batch low-intensity tasks together to take advantage of economies of scale and to reduce distraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group administrative or shallow tasks (email, minor chores) into dedicated blocks so they don't interrupt deep research time; exploit batching to improve concentration and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't base career decisions on glamour or fame; study at different places
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame. But you should study at different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid choosing paths solely for prestige. Still, research training benefits from exposure to different institutions and groups—changing institutions can broaden your network and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming skills: useful but usually not essential for pure mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming is a useful general skill to have, but I think in most areas of pure mathematics it is not necessary (beyond the rudimentary level of skill needed to use mathematical computation packages such as Maple, Mathematica, etc.). In the more numerical parts of applied mathematics programming skills are of course somewhat more essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gain basic competency in mathematical software and programming if useful for experiments or computation, but prioritize the skills most relevant to your subfield; invest more in programming if working in numerical/applied areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to remember and reconstruct proofs by attempting them yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the best ways to memorise the proof of X is to cover up the proof and try to prove it yourself. ... The very best ways to learn the proof of X, of course, are to teach about it in a class, or to adapt that proof for one’s own research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice reconstructing proofs from scratch to internalize the key insights; teaching or adapting proofs for your own work deepens understanding. Focus on the central trick/insight rather than rote memorisation of every step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose graduate programs and advisors carefully if you want a research career
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to work in a flashy area it is most important to work directly under the leader in that area in order to avoid something like this from happening to you. ... It is my feeling that if you want to work in a flashy area it is most important to work directly under the leader in that area in order to avoid ... wasting time proving things that are outdated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for a strong research trajectory, prefer institutions and advisors with active, leading research in your intended area. Being at a top place can reduce risk of working on problems that become quickly outdated; balance this against personal circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build your own network of colleagues and collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: One more (perhaps obvious) bit of career advice: build your own network of colleagues and collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively cultivate professional relationships through conferences, seminars, collaborations, and informal contacts. A network supports idea exchange, joint projects, and career opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt study practices that emphasize active engagement (notes, examples, attempting proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different study methods: take notes; try to solve theorems/propositions before reading solutions; work out your own examples; some retype notes to make them tidy—choose methods that fit you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active study: solve problems before reading solutions, write out examples, and take notes that force you to engage. Tailor study habits to efficiency and depth—some methods cost time but enhance learning; choose accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay attention to time management as a research mathematician
rubrics_metrics.description: I am also (slowly) in the process of gathering my thoughts on time management from the perspective of a research mathematician. Here are some general thoughts on this topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop strategies (batching, focused blocks, prioritization) to protect deep work time and manage teaching/admin duties; experiment to find what scheduling approaches support sustained research productivity.
